source: Fugelsang, Stein, Green, Dunbar (2004) Theory and data interactions of the scientific mind
finding: In three molecular biology labs, over half of results went against the scientists' predictions. Most were first blamed on method, not theory.
numbers: 12 lab meetings, 28 projects, 165 experiments, 417 results; 223 (53%) inconsistent. 196 of 223 got a methodological explanation, 27 a theoretical one.
limits: Observational coding of 3 labs at one US university; coder judgments; method blame is often right because the lab error base rate is high.
agent_relevance: A single anomaly should first trigger a cheap check of method and instruments, not an immediate reframe. Fits a staged S6 trigger.

source: Fugelsang, Stein, Green, Dunbar (2004) Theory and data interactions of the scientific mind
finding: Repeated anomalies change the response. Theory changes rose sharply once an inconsistent finding was replicated.
numbers: Theory modification 12% (27/223) on first inconsistent observation vs 61% of replicated inconsistent findings. Of 84 anomalous replications, 51 theoretical vs 33 methodological explanations.
limits: Percentages as reported by authors; replication was the scientists' own repeat experiments, not controlled.
agent_relevance: Make the impasse trigger count-based: reframe (O8) only after the same anomaly reproduces under a changed check. A threshold idea, not calibrated.

source: Fugelsang, Stein, Green, Dunbar (2004) Theory and data interactions of the scientific mind
finding: Lab simulation with students (causal ratings). Data that clash with an implausible theory were discounted at first. More trials reduced the discounting.
numbers: N=32 (25 F, 7 M, mean age 21.31). Plausibility main effect F(2,62)=21.87, eta2=.41 (implausible 2.52, neutral 3.07, plausible 3.31). Data strength F(1,31)=269.11. Plausibility x Strength F(2,62)=9.83, eta2=.24. Discrimination for low-plausibility theories grew with sample size 10 to 40, F(3,93)=3.16.
limits: Small student sample, made-up pill-and-mood scenario, rating scale; not real discovery.
agent_relevance: Prior plausibility changes how much an anomaly counts. A scaffold should pool evidence over repeated trials, not one look.

source: Trickett, Trafton, Schunn, Harrison (2001) That's odd! How scientists respond to anomalous data
finding: In-vivo analysis of working scientists doing data analysis. They noticed anomalies and gave them more attention than expected results, unlike the confirmation-bias literature.
numbers: 3 scientists (2 astronomers, 1 physicist). Astronomy 27 noticings, 33% anomalous; physics 9 noticings, 44% anomalous. Later references per noticed item: astronomy 7.6 anomalies vs 1.5 expected; physics 3.0 vs 1.25 (t(28)=2.33, p<.05). Hypotheses proposed more often for anomalies, chi2(1)=7.5.
quote: at least one-third of the phenomena the astronomers identified and almost one-half the physicist identified were unusual
limits: Tiny N (3 people; sessions of 53 and 15 min); astronomers shared a dataset; elaboration came mostly from the display, not theory.
agent_relevance: Surprise attracts attention when visible in the data. The agent needs an explicit step that lists surprises in tool output.

source: Trickett et al. (2001), source of elaboration
finding: Scientists explained anomalies mostly by comparing with other data in the display (local context), not by recalling domain theory. In astronomy, 4 of 5 hypotheses about anomalies drew on visual evidence.
numbers: Astronomy: 4 of 5 anomaly hypotheses grounded in the display.
limits: Counts tiny; physics had too few elaborated hypotheses to analyze.
agent_relevance: First reframe candidates may come from contrasting nearby data, not from recalling theory.

source: Fugelsang & Dunbar (2005) Brain-based mechanisms underlying complex causal thinking
finding: fMRI follow-up of the causal-rating paradigm. Search summary: judging data that clash with a plausible theory recruited anterior cingulate, left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and precuneus.
numbers: Not extracted at number level; I downloaded the text but did not read results.
limits: Neuroimaging; reverse inference risk. Region list comes from a search summary.
agent_relevance: Low direct use. Suggests inconsistency detection is a distinct step.

source: Dunbar (1995/1997) lab-meeting studies, as reported in Fugelsang et al. 2004 and Trickett et al. 2001
finding: Dunbar's in-vivo work is the base for the 417-result count. Per Trickett et al., individual scientists were quick to discard a hypothesis when results clashed with it.
numbers: See b01. Dunbar 1997 first-hand numbers not read.
limits: Second-hand. 'Quick discard' (individual) and 'conservative revision' (lab, first sighting) look in tension and depend on level and repeat count.
agent_relevance: Do not hard-code one response; condition on repeat count and on whether the anomaly was checked.

source: Chinn & Brewer (1993) The role of anomalous data in knowledge acquisition
finding: Review proposing 7 responses to anomalous data (ignore, reject, exclude, hold in abeyance, reinterpret, peripheral theory change, theory change). Only the last is full acceptance.
numbers: 7 response types (one accepts and changes theory, six protect it). Eight hypothesised moderating factors. Search snippet only.
limits: Not opened. Taxonomy from a literature review, not one experiment.
agent_relevance: Use as a checklist of ways an agent can dodge an anomaly. The scaffold can detect each dodge in text (for example 'probably noise').

source: Chinn & Brewer (1998) An empirical test of a taxonomy of responses to anomalous data in science
finding: Empirical test of the 1993 taxonomy. Results generally supported it and added one more response type (8 total).
numbers: 8 response types after revision. No sample sizes obtained.
limits: Not opened; sample and effect sizes unknown to me.
agent_relevance: Treat the 8-type list as provisional. Fetch the paper before relying on numbers.

source: Gershman (2019) How to never be wrong
finding: Bayesian analysis of the Duhem problem. One anomaly is rationally shared between central and auxiliary hypotheses, so protecting a theory with auxiliaries can be rational, not only bias. Links to Lakatos protective belt and Kuhn.
numbers: Le Verrier: Neptune worked (Uranus anomaly), Vulcan failed (Mercury perihelion); general relativity later explained Mercury without a new planet.
quote: Bayesian models are falsifiable, because their key predictions are not particular beliefs but particular regularities in belief updating
limits: Theory paper; he says a systematic empirical test of the auxiliary account 'has yet to be undertaken'. People do not follow Bayes rule exactly.
agent_relevance: Credit assignment is the core of an impasse. O8 should ask which assumption the anomaly hits and rank by how firm each is, instead of dropping the whole frame.

source: Gershman (2019), education and developmental evidence
finding: Interventions that help theory change, taken from Chinn & Brewer: build background knowledge first, give an intelligible plausible alternative theory, raise credibility of the anomalous data, avoid ambiguity, use multiple lines of evidence. Children protect prior beliefs with auxiliaries (earth is disk-shaped; tiny unobservable time difference in falling blocks).
numbers: No effect sizes in this passage. Chinn & Brewer p.2 quoted: students discount anomalous data, preserving preinstructional theories.
limits: Secondary summary of classroom work. Alternative-theory advantage is a recommendation here, not a measured effect.
agent_relevance: Reframing needs a ready alternative frame. Offer O8 candidate frames before it drops the old one.

source: Kuhn (1962) The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (as quoted in Gershman 2019)
finding: Kuhn: observation is theory-laden. What a person sees depends on what they look at and on earlier visual-conceptual experience. Anomalies are noticed against a paradigm.
numbers: Quote from p.113 as cited. The oxygen case itself was not read.
quote: What a man sees depends both upon what he looks at and also upon what his previous visual-conceptual experience has taught him to see
limits: Book not opened. Gershman adds Galileo's telescope and Rutherford-Pettersson (Pettersson's assistants reported flashes even when no particles could be emitted) to show observation reports can be unreliable.
agent_relevance: An anomaly may be a measurement fault. Verify the instrument before reframing. The agent's own reading of tool output is also theory-laden.

source: Ríos-García et al. (2026) AI scientists produce results without reasoning scientifically
finding: Large trace analysis of LLM science agents across 8 domains. Agents often fail to use contradicting evidence.
numbers: More than 25,000 runs. Evidence not taken up in 68% of traces. Beliefs never updated in 71%. Refutation-driven belief revision in 26%. Untested claims 53% (63% in hypothesis-driven domains). Convergent multi-test evidence 7%. Explained variance: base model 41.4%, environment scope 30.1%, scaffold 1.5%.
limits: Annotation pipeline is partly automated; models include GPT-4o, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, GPT-OSS-120B; the small scaffold share applies to their scaffolds, not to all possible ones.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that anomaly uptake fails by default. The S6 trigger must be code-checked (compare predicted and observed) because the model rarely revises alone.

source: Ríos-García et al. (2026), per-model table H.16
finding: Refutation-driven belief revision differs by model.
numbers: Fraction of traces: Claude-4.5-Sonnet 0.17, GPT-4o 0.07, GPT-OSS-120B 0.04.
limits: Other rows of the table were garbled by PDF layout and are not quoted.
agent_relevance: Even the best model here revises in only 17% of traces, so put the trigger in code.

source: Wiemann, Smith, Melchior et al. (2026) DiscoverPhysics
finding: Interactive benchmark: 22 simulated worlds with deliberately unusual physics. Eleven frontier models; the strongest pass about half and fail where latent structure must be inferred (hidden particle species, dark-matter-like).
numbers: Eleven models, up to 16 rounds. On the 11 paper worlds, pass rate 45% (Opus 4.7) and 64% (GPT-5.5). Failed runs analysed: 30 of 55 and 20 of 55. Open models lag: gpt-oss-120b 0.22, Llama-3.3-70B 0.10 on the main score.
quote: latent structure is often missed in the first place
limits: Failure classification used Opus 4.7 as judge, one of the subjects. The layer table is garbled in my text, so counts are not quoted.
agent_relevance: Hidden-structure worlds are the paradigm-shift analog. An agent bound to its prior never considers the right class of law. O8 should force a search over new hypothesis classes when a residual stays large.

source: Wiemann et al. (2026) DiscoverPhysics, failure layers
finding: Authors define a self-monitoring failure: the agent produced or received a contradiction (bad residual, derivation pointing elsewhere) and did not act. Opus failures spread over experiment design, signal vs noise and knowing when to stop; GPT-5.5 failures concentrate on never considering the right kind of law.
numbers: Qualitative reading; layer counts not parsed.
limits: LLM-judged classification.
agent_relevance: Two failure types need two fixes: unacted contradictions (code check) and missing hypothesis class (forced alternatives).

source: Zhao et al. (2026) EvoSCM: scientific belief revision through causal model evolution
finding: Scaffold that keeps competing causal-model hypotheses, chooses experiments that separate them, and distils prediction-observation discrepancies into correction rules. Large gains on DiscoverPhysics.
numbers: Explanation score GPT-5.4: baseline 39.80%, EvoSCM 65.30%; GPT-5.5: 51.64% to 75.09%. pass@1 GPT-5.5 7.27% to 56.36%. Ablation (GPT-5.5): free-form text hypotheses 48.18%; random action 47.45%; free-form SCM rewriting 70.73%. Population K=1 63.27%, K=4 74.86%, K=6 75.09%.
limits: Preprint; authors built and tuned on this benchmark; other evolution baselines (GEPA, ReasoningBank, ModelSMC, PiEvo) sometimes scored below the plain baseline.
agent_relevance: Closest working example of an O8 loop: rival frames, discriminating tests, rules from discrepancies. One hypothesis instead of several loses about 12 points, so keep rivals alive.

source: Agarwal et al. (2026) Evidence-informed LLM beliefs for continual scientific discovery
finding: Bayesian surprise (belief shift after evidence) works as an anomaly signal for search. With a static LLM prior, many surprises are not new, since earlier results already imply them.
numbers: 37.5% of static surprisals judged spurious with evidence-informed priors; experts found 29.54% (of 44) and 25% (of 32) of hypotheses called surprising were derivable from prior discoveries; method raised accumulated non-stationary surprisal 30.62% across 5 domains; embedding RAG best anticipated posteriors.
limits: Prior elicited from an LLM; small expert sets.
agent_relevance: Measure anomalies against beliefs updated in this run, or the agent logs false impasses on old news.

source: Trehan & Chopra (2026) Why LLMs aren't scientists yet: four autonomous research attempts
finding: Four end-to-end autonomous ML paper attempts. Three failed in implementation or evaluation; one was accepted at Agents4Science 2025. Six failure modes, including overexcitement: declaring success despite obvious failures.
numbers: 4 attempts, 1 completed; 6 failure modes.
limits: Case study N=4, one pipeline, no controls.
agent_relevance: An agent may explain away anomalies in its own results as success. Compare run output against stated predictions in code.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to falsify
finding: Eleven LLMs on a Wason 2-4-6 style rule task with feedback. Models favour confirming tests, which slows rule discovery. Prompting for disconfirmation helps.
numbers: Success 6% to 78% across models (max 45 turns). Average rule discovery 42% to 56% with the counter-example prompt. Confirmation bias correlates negatively with success; thinking models do better, but not through a consistent rise in incompatible-test ratio.
limits: Toy rule task; distilled behavior transferred to Blicket tests.
agent_relevance: A cheap step that asks for a test the current frame says should fail is worth about +14 points on average here. Use before calling a frame settled.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Self-correction without external labels does not help reasoning and often hurts. Earlier gains came from oracle labels telling the model when it was wrong.
numbers: Intrinsic self-correction lowers accuracy on GSM8K and CommonSenseQA; GPT-3.5 keeps its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time and, when it changes, more often goes right to wrong. GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K 91.5 baseline, 88.0 after round 1, 90.0 after round 2.
limits: 2023-era models, 3 benchmarks; newer reasoning models may differ.
agent_relevance: The model cannot tell alone whether a step is an anomaly. The signal must come from outside: tests, code, mismatch counts.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld
finding: Virtual environment with 120 discovery tasks in 8 themes (one involves finding the anomalous species). GPT-4o agents do poorly end to end; expert humans do much better.
numbers: 11 human scientists: completion 66%, knowledge 55%. Best agent (ReAct) completed 38% of easy and 18% of challenge tasks; best explanatory knowledge (Hypothesizer) 34% easy, 8% challenge. Unit-test sub-skills about 60%+ completion.
limits: One model (GPT-4o), zero-shot; humans had one seed and a 1-hour limit.
agent_relevance: Sub-skills like measuring are fine; the gap is turning anomalies into explanation. Supports a staged loop over a flat ReAct loop.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench
finding: Equation discovery benchmark with transformed and synthetic problems. Best system reaches about 31% symbolic accuracy; all methods do worse out of domain.
numbers: Best system 31.5% symbolic accuracy (abstract); 28.1% on LSR-Synth per intro text.
limits: Table cells not parsed; abstract-level claims.
agent_relevance: Fitting known data is easy, recovering the right structure is not. Supports using out-of-domain residuals as the anomaly detector.

source: Banatt et al. (2024) WILT; Bertolazzi et al. (2026) FalsifyBench (search summary)
finding: WILT multi-turn inductive task (up to 30 tests) and FalsifyBench report low LLM success when the true rule is broader than the first example.
numbers: No numbers obtained.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Secondary support for forced counter-example tests.

source: Kulkarni & Simon (1988) KEKADA, as cited by Trickett et al. 2001
finding: KEKADA modelled Krebs' urea-cycle discovery; an 'attend to surprising result' heuristic was crucial.
numbers: Qualitative citation only.
limits: Original not read.
agent_relevance: Oldest working model of anomaly-driven discovery: surprise triggers focused follow-up, matching S6 then O8.

source: Alberdi, Sleeman, Korpi (2000), as cited by Trickett et al. 2001
finding: Expert botanists on a categorisation task attended to 'rogue' items. Main strategy: instantiate, i.e. search domain knowledge for a new hypothesis that fits the anomaly.
numbers: Qualitative citation; no N.
limits: Second-hand; categorisation, not experiments.
agent_relevance: Reframe by searching a stored hypothesis library first, then invent new classes.

source: Ríos-García et al. (2026) as cited in DiscoverPhysics related work
finding: A second paper confirms the point: outcome scores hide missing belief revision. Agents reach correct answers while ignoring evidence.
numbers: 68% evidence ignored and 26% refutation-driven revision, even when agents arrive at correct answers (as stated in DiscoverPhysics text).
limits: A citation, not an independent replication.
agent_relevance: Log revision events, not only final accuracy, when measuring the scaffold.

source: Oxygen case and historical critiques of Kuhn (gap)
finding: No primary source on Lavoisier, Priestley or Scheele was opened. Nearest opened case of one anomaly with two resolutions: Neptune (new object, right) and Vulcan (new object, wrong; solved by a new theory).
numbers: Neptune vs Vulcan, both from the Gershman text.
limits: Gap: no opened account of the oxygen case or of Laudan and Lakatos critiques.
agent_relevance: The same anomaly can support 'add auxiliary' or 'change frame'. A discriminating test should separate them, as EvoSCM does.

source: Lakatos (1976) as discussed in Gershman 2019
finding: Lakatos: a research programme is kept while it adds novel corroborated predictions; auxiliaries form a protective belt.
numbers: Qualitative.
limits: Book not opened; second-hand.
agent_relevance: Possible rule: count novel predictions per patch; if none after a few patches, move to reframe. Untested design idea.
